Correlation Heatmap
Full matrix — how every pair moves relative to every other pair
📖 How to read the Correlation Heatmap:
Correlations are computed on each bar's % move (log return), not on price levels — so a high number means the pairs genuinely move together bar-by-bar, not merely that both drifted the same way over the window. On this scale honest FX numbers run lower than the levels-based readings shown before V371: ±40 is moderate, ±60 is strong, ±80 is very strong.
🟢 Green = Positive correlation (+40 to +100) — both pairs move in the same direction. Example: EURUSD and GBPUSD typically read around +65 because both rise when USD weakens. Risk: buying both doubles your USD exposure — not diversifying, you're stacking the same bet.
🔴 Red = Negative correlation (−40 to −100) — the pairs move in opposite directions. Example: EURUSD and USDCHF typically read around −80 because when EUR/USD rises, USD/CHF falls. Useful for hedging — a long on one partially offsets a long on the other.
⬜ Grey = Weak/neutral (−40 to +40) — little to no consistent relationship. These pairs move mostly independently.
The number is the Pearson correlation coefficient from −100 (perfect opposite) to +100 (perfect same direction), measured on the loaded window — it is an estimate, not a constant, and it shifts with market regime.
⚠ Important: This tells you about co-movement only — NOT buy/sell direction. A +80 means the pairs move together in percentage terms. It does not tell you whether to buy or sell either pair. Use the Bias Scanner and Trade Ideas for direction signals.

🎯 Views: Bar Chart = all pairs ranked by retail positioning. Area Chart = sentiment trend over time per pair. Gauge = single pair contrarian signal.

Confluence Scanner
Start with a currency bias — find every pair that confirms or opposes that view
📖 Confluence Scanner vs Correlation Trade Report — what's the difference?
Correlation Trade Report answers: "I want to trade EURUSD — what other pairs move with it?" You start with a pair.
Confluence Scanner answers: "I think USD is going to strengthen — which pairs confirm that theme?" You start with a currency.

🎯 How to use it: If your analysis (fundamental, COT, sentiment) tells you USD is bullish, select USD. The scanner shows every pair where buying/selling that pair = expressing a USD bullish view. The more pairs that confirm (direct + peer), the higher your conviction. When 5+ pairs all point to USD strength, that's confluence — not just a single signal.

Divergence Detector
Pairs that historically move together but are currently separating — high-probability mean reversion setups
📖 What is correlation divergence and why does it matter?
Two pairs like EURUSD and GBPUSD might normally move together 85% of the time (historically correlated). If suddenly over the past 2 weeks EURUSD is falling sharply while GBPUSD is rising — that's a divergence. One of them is "wrong" relative to the historical relationship and will likely snap back to realign.

🎯 How to trade it: When a divergence is detected, the pair that has moved MOST from its historical position is the likely candidate to reverse. Look at both pairs — the one with the bigger recent move is your fade candidate. Wait for price action confirmation (a pin bar, engulfing, or break of structure) before entering.

Example: EURUSD normally correlates +65% with GBPUSD. Over the recent window the correlation dropped to +10%. EURUSD fell 200 pips while GBPUSD only fell 30 pips. GBPUSD has "under-performed" the relationship — it should have fallen more. Fade: SELL GBPUSD expecting it to catch down to EURUSD.

Precision note: the recent reading uses the last ~15 moves, and a correlation from 15 points carries a margin of roughly ±45. A gap smaller than that can be pure sampling noise — treat sub-threshold divergences as watchlist material, and require price-action confirmation before trading any of them.

Pivot Points
Floor trader pivots, Fibonacci pivots and key S/R levels calculated from price data
📖 How pivot points work: Pivot points are price levels calculated from the previous day's High, Low, and Close. Banks and institutional traders use these exact same levels as targets and stops — making them self-fulfilling. PP = the main pivot (like a magnet). S1/S2/S3 = support levels below. R1/R2/R3 = resistance levels above. Price tends to gravitate toward PP and bounce or break at S/R levels.
Load price data first, then pivots calculate automatically.
Index Pivot Intelligence
Monitor index pivot levels → cross-reference with forex pairs → generate high-probability trade signals
📡 How Index Pivot Intelligence works:
Indices like DXY (US Dollar Index) and the other currency indices (EXY, BXY, JXY, SXY, AXY, CXY, ZXY) plus equity indices (SPX500, NAS100, etc.) are leading indicators for forex. When an index hits a key pivot level, it signals a likely reaction in correlated currency pairs.
• DXY hitting R1/R2/R3 = USD showing resistance → BUY EURUSD, GBPUSD, AUDUSD (USD likely to weaken)
• DXY hitting S1/S2/S3 = USD at support → SELL EURUSD, GBPUSD (USD likely to strengthen)
• SPX/NAS at Support = Risk-off potential → Buy JPY/CHF, Sell AUD/NZD/CAD
• SPX/NAS at Resistance = Risk-on potential → Buy AUD/NZD/CAD, Sell JPY/CHF
🔥 Cross-Index Confluence (high-probability signal): When two currency indices agree on a pair direction — e.g. DXY at S2 (USD strong) + EXY at R2 (EUR peaked) both imply EUR/USD SELL — a flashing red toast appears. These are your highest-probability setups, fired once per day per confluence.
Real vs Synthetic data: Currency indices try Twelve Data's real symbols first; if your plan doesn't carry them, they fall back to synthetic versions computed from your loaded forex pairs. Each chart shows ✓ REAL or ≈ SYNTH so you know what you're looking at. Synthetic versions track ~90% of real movement.

🎯 Best approach: Use these signals as a bias filter — when an index is at a pivot, look for price action confirmation (engulfing, pin bar) on the corresponding forex pair before entering.

🎯 Confluence Score
Aggregates rate diff · real yields · index pivots · COT positioning · strength · risk regime · news proximity into a single -100 to +100 readiness score per pair
📊 How the Confluence Score works:
The score combines independent signals from across the platform. Each factor adds points (positive = BUY bias, negative = SELL bias). The total ranges from −90 to +90 across 7 factors (rate diff, real yields, index pivots, COT positioning, currency strength, risk regime, retail sentiment). A score above +45 means many factors agree on BUY; below −45 means many agree on SELL. Between −22 and +22 means signals are conflicting — sit on hands.
⚠ News block: If a high-impact event for either currency is within 30 minutes, the pair shows BLOCKED regardless of score — never trade into news.
Honest limits: This is a confluence checker, not a prediction model. It tells you when independent signals align. It does NOT predict price. Always confirm with price action before entering.

Candlestick Bias Scanner
Engulfing candles across timeframes — institutional macro directional bias
📖 How the Bias Scanner works:
⚠ Only fully closed candles are read — the current open candle is always skipped.
The scanner walks back through history to find the most recent valid engulfing for each timeframe — however far back it needs to go. That signal remains the active bias until a new opposing engulfing closes and overrides it.

✅ BUY signal — last closed signal candle's body closed above the reference candle's High
✅ SELL signal — last closed signal candle's body closed below the reference candle's Low

🎯 High probability: Monthly + Weekly aligned = strongest macro bias. Weekly + Daily = medium-term. H4 is excluded (requires separate data fetch).

📈 Three-Stage Confluence Scanner
EMA trend + CCI cycle + MACD trigger across M1, W1, D1, H4, H1 — high-probability entry confirmation
⏰ Auto-refresh:
Every:
Active hours (SAST): to
Idle
📖 Three-stage confluence system:

Stage 1 — EMA Trend (50/150/250): Bullish when 50>150>250 with meaningful separation. Bearish when 50<150<250. Otherwise MIXED.
Stage 2 — CCI Confirmation (Length 20, SMA-14 smoothed): Looks at the MOST RECENT CCI extreme. For a buy setup (EMA bullish), CCI's last extreme must have been oversold (closed below −100) — price exhausted to the downside, now recovering. For a sell setup (EMA bearish), last extreme must have been overbought (above +100). Matches TradingView CCI defaults so signals align with your charts.
Stage 3 — MACD Histogram Trigger (12/26/9): For sells, first lower positive bar after a rising sequence (bullish momentum waning). For buys, first higher negative bar after a falling sequence. MACD only counts if it triggered AFTER CCI confirmation. Once fired, the trigger stays valid as long as the foundation holds — i.e., EMA bias intact AND CCI confirmation not invalidated by an opposite extreme. The histogram crossing zero after the trigger is just confirmation that the move is underway, not invalidation.

🔥 FULL TRIGGER = HIGH PROBABILITY: all three stages confirmed and aligned. Plays alert sound on fresh MACD trigger only.
📊 Stage column: shows how many TFs are at each stage. "🔥 N/5 FULL" = N timeframes fully triggered. "N CCI prep" = waiting for MACD.
⏰ Fire on close only: cross events and MACD triggers use the last CLOSED candle, never the in-progress one. The status column shows live alignment.

Honest caveats: All three indicators lag price — FULL triggers fire after momentum has already turned. Useful for confirming entries, not predicting tops/bottoms. M1 250-EMA needs ~250 months of history; some pairs may show "insufficient data".

🎯 Positioning Index (0–100) — Divergence Spotter
Each line scaled to its own high/low over the chosen window
Green = bullish read · Red = bearish read. NC (Leveraged Funds) is read directionally — the direction driver; a high net-long reading is bullish (green). COMM (Commercials) is value / reversal context — it confirms when aligned with NC and flags a reversal-watch at an extreme opposite (not a standalone direction). NR (retail) is the crowd, read contrarian — a high NR reading is a crowded / caution signal (red). When COMM or NR diverge from the NC direction, that's your setup. Free · No API key needed · Updates every Friday
Data: CFTC Public Reporting API · Released every Friday 3:30pm EST · Reflects previous Tuesday positions · Non-Commercial = Large speculators/hedge funds  ·  Commercial = Hedgers (banks/corporations)  ·  Non-Reportable = Retail (positions below CFTC threshold)  ·  52W Index = where current net sits in the 52-week range (100 = max long, 0 = max short)
📖 How to read this COT table — Full Guide Non-Comm Net (Change ▲▼): Net long contracts held by large speculators (hedge funds). Positive = net long (bullish), negative = net short (bearish). The Change shows how much the position shifted week-on-week — a large increase means smart money is aggressively adding. This is the most powerful signal.
Comm Net (Change ▲▼): Commercial hedgers — in FX futures, this category includes major global banks, multinational corporates, and central banks. In FX, commercial positioning has historically correlated positively with future returns (Klitgaard & Weir 2004; Wang 2003), but this platform uses commercials as a VALUE / reversal-context input rather than the direction driver: when commercials align with the Leveraged Funds (NC) direction, that's institutional confirmation; when they sit at an extreme opposite, that flags a mature trend / reversal watch. Note: in commodities the opposite (contrarian) interpretation applies — commercials there are the contrarian smart money.
52W Index (0–100): Where current Non-Comm net positioning sits within the past 52-week range. 90–100 = EXTREME LONG (crowded — watch for reversal). 0–10 = EXTREME SHORT (potential bottom). 40–60 = neutral.
Signal: Bullish = speculators increasing net long. Bearish = net turning negative. Extreme = 52W beyond 85/15 — historically precedes mean-reversion.
📊 52W Index Guide: 0 = positioning at 52-week LOW (extreme short) · 100 = positioning at 52-week HIGH (extreme long). Sweet spot for trend following: 30–70 (not yet extreme). Above 80 or below 20 = crowded = higher reversal risk. When 52W is below 20 AND Commercials are net long = classic SHORT TRAP.

🎯 Trading use: Find currencies where Non-Comm is rising AND 52W is 30–70 (not yet extreme) — sweet spot for trend following. Pair with a weakening currency (high 52W or turning bearish). The bigger the weekly Change, the more institutional urgency behind the move.

📖 How to read sentiment — Direct vs Contrarian (toggle above):
DIRECT (your current default): the crowd’s majority side is treated as the signal — 65% long counts as bullish pressure. This is how every scorer on the platform now reads it, based on your own tested results.
CONTRARIAN (the classic textbook read): retail is statistically wrong at extremes — 75%+ LONG suggests institutions are selling to them, 75%+ SHORT suggests institutions are buying. Strongest as a fade signal only at stretched levels, and when COT commercials sit on the opposite side.
The toggle switches the whole platform between these two readings — Probability Scanner, Confluence, Trade Ideas, Position Book layers and the COT Sheet comparison all follow it, so no page ever argues with another.
The Avg Long/Short Price shows where the crowd entered — price often moves toward these levels to hunt stops before reversing.
🎯 Best signals: Look for pairs where >70% are on one side AND the avg entry price is far from current price — those traders are sitting in large drawdown and likely to panic-close soon.

📖 Position Book
Where the retail crowd is positioned vs where smart money (COT) sits — fused into one view to spot high-conviction fades
What this is: A crowd-vs-smart-money position book built from live Myfxbook retail positioning (long/short volume, position counts, average entry prices) cross-referenced with COT institutional data. The edge: a raw order book only shows the crowd. This shows you when the crowd is heavily positioned and smart money disagrees — the setups worth fading. Requires Myfxbook connected (Sentiment tab) and COT data loaded (COT Report tab).
📘 How to use this page (and how to read the order book) — click to open
The quick workflow
1. Connect Myfxbook (Sentiment tab) and load COT (COT Report tab).
2. Pick a pair from the dropdown.
3. Read the verdict banner at the top — it's the one-line takeaway.
4. Switch signal layers (below) to see the setup from different angles. More stars = more reliable.
5. For crypto pairs, scroll down to the real order book.
The two cards (Crowd vs Smart Money)
👥 The Crowd = retail traders (Myfxbook). Green bar = % long, red = % short. The crowd is usually wrong at extremes — when 70%+ pile one way, the market often goes the other.
🏛 Smart Money = COT institutions. This platform uses NC (Leveraged Funds) as the direction driver (their positioning is the trend) and COMM (Commercials) as value / fade context. The classic fade setup is when the retail crowd is stretched one way and the institutions lean the other.
The signal layers (by accuracy)
🔥 Squeeze Fuel ★★★★★ — measured fact. Shows if the crowd's average entry is underwater. Trapped traders panic-close, which fuels a move. A trapped long crowd selling pushes price DOWN; trapped shorts buying pushes UP. Most trustworthy because it's data, not theory.
🏛 Crowd vs COMM ★★★★ — your main fade signal: crowd stretched one way + commercials leaning the other. Weekly data, so up to 3 days old.
🎯 Multi-Pair Scan ★★★ — ranks every pair by fade conviction. A hunting tool; click a row to open that pair. Surfaces weaker setups too, so confirm with the higher-star layers.
🐎 NC Fast Money ★★ — large speculators. Noisy. Best used only as confirmation: if it agrees with COMM, extra confidence; if not, caution.
Estimated price ladder (FX)
A modelled picture of where longs (green, right) and shorts (red, left) likely sit, spread around their average entries. The dashed line is current price. ⚠ This is an estimate, not a real book — Myfxbook only gives one average entry per side. Use it to visualise roughly where the crowd is, not as precise levels.
📊 Reading the REAL order book (crypto only) ★★★★★
For BTC, ETH, SOL etc. you get Binance's live depth-of-market — actual resting limit orders, not a model. How to read it:
• Asks (top, red) = sell orders sitting above current price. A big red bar = a sell wall — lots of supply there; price often struggles to break above it (acts as resistance).
• Bids (bottom, green) = buy orders sitting below price. A big green bar = a buy wall — strong demand; price often bounces off it (acts as support).
• Bar length = how much volume is resting at that price. Longer = more orders = a more significant level.
• Spread = gap between the best bid and best ask. Tight = liquid/easy fills; wide = thin/volatile.
• How to trade it: walls show where big players are willing to buy/sell. Price tends to gravitate toward liquidity and stall at walls. But note walls can be pulled (spoofing) — treat them as context, not guarantees. Big wall above + you're long → consider taking profit before it. Big wall below + you're short → cover before it.
⚠ Reminder: retail/COT data is a representative sample, not the whole market. The crypto order book is real but only Binance's book. None of this is financial advice — it's context to inform your own decisions.

How direction is decided: NC (Leveraged Funds) = direction driver (net long → bullish) · COMM = value/context (aligned → confirmation, extreme opposite → reversal watch) · NR & Retail Sentiment = contrarian (crowded → faded). The Positioning Index card now reads NC and COMM directionally and NR contrarian — consistent with this framework (all lines show bullish/bearish for price).
Click Calculate — COT data will load automatically if needed.
Institutional Composite Score
📖 How to read this chart: The green/red/gold bars are the composite score per currency — taller green = stronger institutional bullish bias, deeper red = stronger bearish bias. The NC line shows Leveraged-Funds positioning — the direction driver. Comm is value / confirmation context: it reinforces the NC direction when aligned and flags a reversal-watch when at an extreme opposite (weight scales 10%→35% at NC extremes). NR is small retail (contrarian only at extremes). Sentiment is the inverted Myfxbook reading. 🎯 High probability trade: Tallest green bar vs deepest red bar — confluence of all three COT lines pointing the same direction = highest conviction. Click toggles above to show/hide each component. Lines fade when their current weight is low (non-extreme NC = Comm has only 10% influence). TRAP signals fire when NC is at an extreme but Commercials sit OPPOSITE — a mature/exhausted trend where the crowd of speculators is stretched against the value side.

🧠 Index IQ
Constituent order flow · Weighted pressure score · Divergence detection · Smart money signals
🧠 How Index IQ Works
The Core Idea: Major indices like NAS100 are driven by their top weighted stocks. If Apple, Microsoft and NVIDIA are all sitting at key support levels simultaneously, NAS100 almost certainly bounces — because those 3 stocks alone represent ~24% of the entire index.
Weighted Pressure Score: Each top constituent is analysed against its D1/H4 pivot points and swing levels. Stocks near support = bullish pressure weighted by their index %. Stocks near resistance = bearish pressure. The sum gives a score from -100 (heavy sell pressure) to +100 (heavy buy pressure).
Constituent Divergence: When an index makes a new high but only 2 or 3 stocks are driving it (the others are lagging or at resistance), that's distribution — smart money is selling into the strength. This is invisible on the index chart alone.
Alert Threshold: Set your score threshold — when the weighted pressure crosses it, you get an alert with the exact stocks causing the move.
Every Active to SAST Idle
Load price data (Refresh Data) then click 🧠 Scan All Indices.
⚠ Constituent Divergence Signals
Detected when index price action disagrees with constituent stock positioning — smart money distribution/accumulation signals

💰 Index Valuation — cheap or expensive?
A valuation tool answers a different question from the rest of Index IQ: not "where is price going next?" but "is the current price justified by underlying earnings?". Enter the P/E and/or CAPE for each index — or use auto-fetch (tries the proxy ETF via FMP) — and the platform shows where it sits vs historical valuation bands. Valuation is slow context, not a timing signal — an index can stay expensive for years.
Where to get the numbers manually (free, ~2 min/month): trailing P/E and CAPE for the S&P 500 at multpl.com. For other indices, P/E is on the proxy-ETF pages (QQQ, SPY, DIA). CAPE barely moves week-to-week — updating monthly is fine.
📊 Index Value Score — one number from the valuation inputs
Turns the P/E and CAPE you entered above — plus the equity risk premium (how much extra return stocks offer over the 10-year bond) — into a single −100 to +100 value score. Positive = cheap/attractive (multi-year tailwind); negative = expensive/stretched (multi-year headwind). This is a slow, valuation-based bias, the opposite end of the spectrum from your pivots — it tells you the long-run wind direction, not the next move.
Enter P/E and/or CAPE above (or auto-fetch), then click “Compute value score”.
😱 Implied Volatility — the market's fear gauge
ATR tells you how much an index has moved; the volatility indices tell you how much the options market expects it to move — a forward-looking read ATR can't give. Each equity index has its own: VIX (S&P 500), VXN (Nasdaq 100), VXD (Dow). The term structure (VIX vs 3-month VIX3M) is the real institutional signal: contango (near-term cheaper, ratio <1) is the calm default ~80–85% of the time; backwardation (ratio >1) flags acute stress and has preceded most sharp S&P drawdowns.
Click “Load / refresh VIX” to pull live VIX, VXN, VXD and the VIX3M term structure (from FRED via your macro worker — no Twelve Data plan needed).
Reads as a regime, not a timing trigger: a low VIX in steep contango = risk-on backdrop favouring index longs; a rising VIX flipping toward backwardation = risk-off, tighten or stand aside. Pair it with the constituent gauge and pivots — they agree most strongly at turning points.
🌐 Breadth & Risk-Regime — is the move broad or fragile?
An index can rise while most of its stocks fall — a handful of giants masking a weak market. Breadth measures how many constituents actually participate: broad = healthy and durable, narrow = fragile and prone to sharp reversals. Risk-regime reads the macro backdrop — the dollar (DXY) and the 10-year yield — that decides whether equities have a tailwind or headwind. Together they answer "should I trust this move?".
Load constituent data (🧠 Scan All Indices above), then click refresh.
🏛️ Index COT — where the hedge funds are positioned
The CFTC's Traders in Financial Futures report splits the big players into four groups: Dealers (sell-side banks), Asset Managers (pensions/insurers — structurally long), Leveraged Funds (hedge funds/CTAs — the tactical "smart money") and Other. Each card shows all four so you can compare who's long vs short — but the headline read tracks Leveraged Funds, because Asset Managers are long by mandate (not a directional bet) while hedge funds make the tactical calls. The headline shows their net as a 3-year percentile: near 100% = crowded long (contrarian caution); near 0% = crowded short (contrarian opportunity). Released Fridays for the prior Tuesday — a slow, positioning-based signal, not a timing trigger.
Click “Load / refresh COT” to pull the latest CFTC positioning for SPX500, NAS100 and US30.

⚖️ Constituent Strength Gauge
Reads where each top-weighted constituent sits on its own pivot levels, weights it by that stock's pull on the index, and sums the result. Heavy names clustered at resistance = broad sell pressure on the index; clustered at support = broad buy pressure. This is the equity analogue of currency strength — it measures internal breadth, not a two-currency gap.

📐 Strategies
Swing High/Low detection · Auto-Chartist key levels · Session + correlation grouping
📐 Swing Strategy Logic: A D1 Swing High = a candle whose high is higher than the 3 candles before AND after it — meaning it forms on day 3, confirmed on day 4. On day 4 we look for intraday selling opportunities (the swing high is where institutions loaded shorts). A D1 Swing Low = opposite — institutions loaded longs. On day 4 we look for intraday buying opportunities. Results are grouped by session (best time to trade the intraday signal) and correlated pairs (other pairs confirming the move).

🏛️ Institutional Positioning
Daily CME FX futures open interest — where institutional money is building or unwinding. A daily-fresh cousin of the weekly COT report, sourced from real exchange data.
📌 How to read this: Open interest = the number of outstanding futures contracts. Rising OI = fresh positions building (conviction entering); falling OI = positions unwinding (money leaving). This tracks the front-month contract day-over-day. The USD row is synthesized from the other seven (no single dollar contract exists on CME). Updates daily after the US close.
📖 How to use this tool & capitalise from it (full guide)
1. What this data actually is
These are real CME currency futures statistics — the contracts where banks, hedge funds and institutions hedge and speculate on FX. We track open interest (OI): the total number of outstanding contracts. Unlike the weekly COT report (released Friday, 3 days stale), this updates daily after the US close, so it's a fresher read on the same institutional money.
2. What "building" vs "unwinding" means
Building (rising OI): new contracts are being opened — fresh money is entering that currency. This signals conviction: participants are committing capital, not just shuffling existing positions.
Unwinding (falling OI): contracts are being closed — money is leaving. Positions are being exited, which can mean a move is losing steam or a crowd is heading for the door.
Flat (±0–3%): no meaningful change in commitment.
3. THE most important limitation — read this
Open interest tells you CONVICTION, not DIRECTION. Rising OI does not by itself mean "go long." It means money is committing — but you must look at price to know which way. The rule:
Rising OI + rising price  →  bullish conviction (new longs)
Rising OI + falling price  →  bearish conviction (new shorts)
Falling OI + rising price  →  short covering (rally may be weak)
Falling OI + falling price  →  long liquidation (selloff may be weak)
This is why this tool is a confluence input, not a standalone buy/sell signal. It confirms or questions a setup you've found with price action and your other tools — it doesn't generate trades on its own.
4. How to actually capitalise — step by step
Step 1. Look at the USD row first. Since most pairs are vs USD, the dollar's lean frames everything. USD building = headwind for foreign-currency longs; USD unwinding = tailwind.
Step 2. Find the extremes in the ranking — the currency building most and the one unwinding most. The strongest setups pair conviction against exhaustion.
Step 3. Form a pair: a building currency vs an unwinding one (see the Pair Ideas below, which do this for you).
Step 4. Confirm direction with price — check the chart and your Confluence Score for that pair. OI conviction + agreeing price + other tools aligning = a high-quality setup.
Step 5. If OI and price disagree (e.g. price rising but OI falling), treat it as a warning — the move may lack backing. Stand aside or tighten risk.
5. Best practices & honest caveats
• This is a swing/position-trade signal (days-to-weeks), not a scalping tool — OI shifts slowly.
• One day's change can be noise. A multi-day trend in the same direction is far more meaningful than a single reading.
• Quarterly roll weeks (Mar/Jun/Sep/Dec) can distort OI as contracts expire — be more cautious then.
• The USD row is synthetic — inferred from the other seven, weighted like the Dollar Index. It's a strong proxy, not a directly-traded contract.
• Never size a trade on OI alone. Require ≥2 other tools agreeing (price structure, Value, COT, sentiment) before acting.

🏦 Interest Rate Tracker
Central bank policy rates · last changes · upcoming meetings · directional bias implications
📖 Why interest rates drive forex direction
Capital flows toward higher yields. When the Fed pays 3.625% and the BOJ pays 0.75%, big institutional money flows from JPY into USD instruments to capture that 2.875% yield gap. This buying pressure on USD (and selling pressure on JPY) is one of the strongest forex drivers — it's the foundation of the carry trade, where traders borrow in low-yield currencies and invest in high-yield ones.
The three rate signals that matter
  1. Current rate level (the gap): Bigger gap = stronger trend bias. AUD/JPY has a 3.6% gap (4.35% AUD vs 0.75% JPY) — the textbook carry trade. Money is paid to hold this pair long.
  2. Direction of change: A central bank actively HIKING is more bullish than one that's just at high rates. RBA's May 5 hike to 4.35% triggered immediate AUD strength even though the gap with JPY barely moved.
  3. Stance / forward guidance: A "hawkish hold" can rally a currency more than a dovish hike. Watch the language: "data-dependent" = neutral, "vigilant on inflation" = hawkish, "monitoring downside risks" = dovish.
How to actually trade it
Strategy 1 — Carry trade (longer-term, weeks to months): Buy the high-rate currency, sell the low-rate one. You earn the daily swap (rollover interest) while waiting for the trend. Best in calm markets. Example: long AUD/JPY in current rate environment. Risk: when risk-off hits, carry trades unwind violently.

Strategy 2 — Rate decision day trade: Position before the meeting based on consensus expectations. If the bank surprises (hike when hold expected, or vice versa), the currency moves 50-150 pips in seconds. Honest caveat — this is gambling unless you have an edge on positioning data.

Strategy 3 — Convergence/divergence (most reliable): Trade pairs where one bank is hiking while the other is cutting. The differential WIDENS over time, pushing the pair in the direction of the hiking currency. Example: BOJ hiking + BOE cutting = GBP/JPY likely down over weeks. This is what your platform's "Monetary Policy Alignment" check does automatically.
Pitfalls that catch retail traders
  • Rates ≠ instant currency moves. The gap between AUD and JPY rates has been positive for years, but AUD/JPY still has down-weeks. Rates set the BIAS, not the daily direction.
  • Politics overrides math. When markets fear a recession or war, capital flees TO safe-haven low-yield currencies (USD, JPY, CHF) regardless of rate gaps. Risk-off can flip the entire script.
  • Forward guidance often beats current rates. If the BOJ at 0.75% sounds more hawkish than the Fed at 3.625%, JPY can strengthen against USD even though the rate gap favours USD.
  • Carry trades unwind fast. Years of slow accumulation can reverse in weeks during volatility spikes (Aug 2024 yen carry unwind dropped USD/JPY 12% in 6 weeks).
Data is hard-coded and updated manually after each central bank meeting. Last update: early May 2026.
🔄 Market Cycles
COT cycles · Seasonality · Gann Square of 9 · Cycle timing
🔄 How to Use Market Cycles
🟣 Gann Square of 9
What it is: W.D. Gann discovered that price levels derived from square-root mathematics often act as invisible support/resistance. The Gann Square calculates key future price levels and time dates from the current price using 90°, 180°, 270°, 360° rotation points.

How to trade it: When price reaches a Gann level on a Gann time date simultaneously — that's the highest-probability reversal zone. Combine with a D1 pivot point hit for maximum confluence. Works best on indices and gold.
🔵 COT Positioning Cycles
What it is: Every currency cycles through: TROUGH (extreme short) → RISING (institutions accumulating) → PEAK (extreme long) → DECLINING (institutions distributing). The phase is determined by the 52W positioning index.

How to trade it: Enter longs when a currency is in TROUGH→RISING transition. Enter shorts when PEAK→DECLINING. Avoid trading against the COT cycle. Best for swing/position trades (1–8 weeks). Do NOT use for intraday.
🟡 Seasonality Patterns
What it is: Historical average monthly returns by pair, calculated from years of loaded price data. For example, EURUSD has historically risen in Jan/Feb and fallen in Sep/Oct.

How to trade it: Use as a directional bias filter ONLY — never trade seasonality alone. Most powerful when: seasonal bias + COT cycle phase + price at pivot level all agree on the same direction. Best for position trades and swing bias decisions.
💡 Best combination: COT cycle = RISING + Seasonal month is positive + Price hitting Gann level + D1 pivot support = All 4 aligned → highest conviction trade setup possible.

🎯 Time-Cycle Backtest — how accurate are the cycles on this pair?
For every historical swing on the selected pair, this projects each Gann/natural day-count forward and checks whether a real swing actually landed near the projected date. It reports the hit-rate at ±1/±2/±3-day windows, for major and medium swings separately — and crucially, shows two baselines (random dates & the all-day base rate) so you can see the true edge over chance, not just a raw percentage.
